title: Master Headless Tools
objectives: Navigate the Headless Tools directory and filter by category
Evaluate a listing for agent-readiness (docs, auth, machine-readable specs)
Integrate one directory tool into an AI agent via function calling

modules.title: Find and Shortlist Tools
steps: Open headless.tools and filter the directory by one category you'll actually use (e.g., email, payments, or web scraping)
Open 3 listings and record each tool's base API URL, auth method, and free tier limits in a notes file
Discard any listing whose docs require a human UI flow (OAuth consent screens you can't automate, dashboard-only config)

modules.title: Assess Agent-Readiness
steps: For each shortlisted tool, check its docs for an OpenAPI spec, MCP server, or structured JSON error responses — note which exist
Read the rate limits and webhook docs; write down how an agent would retry a 429 and verify a webhook signature
Pick a winner by scoring the 3 tools 1-5 on spec availability, error format, and idempotency-key support

modules.title: Test the API Headlessly
steps: Sign up for your chosen tool, mint an API key, and store it in a .env file (never hardcode it)
Run the docs' 'hello world' endpoint with curl, piping the response through jq to confirm the JSON shape matches the docs
Deliberately send one malformed request and one request without the key; confirm both return machine-readable error codes

modules.title: Wire It Into an Agent
steps: Write a JSON-schema function definition (name, description, parameters) that wraps the endpoint you tested
Register the function with your agent framework (OpenAI tools, Anthropic tool use, or LangChain) and run a prompt that triggers it
Add a guardrail: cap calls per run, and log the agent's raw tool-call arguments for one test session to catch hallucinated parameters

Have built at least a basic AI agent or chatbot with tool/function calling

title: Master Raven
objectives: Embed an AES-encrypted secret message inside innocent cover text with a passphrase
Extract and decrypt a hidden message from received text, verifying integrity
Spot and remove telltale artifacts that reveal a text carries hidden data

modules.title: Install Raven and run your first encode
steps: Install via `pip install raven-stego` and confirm with `raven --version`
Write a one-line secret to secret.txt and a 3-paragraph blog-style sample to cover.txt
Run `raven encode --cover cover.txt --secret secret.txt --passphrase 'correct horse' -o out.txt`, then diff out.txt against cover.txt to see the visible text is unchanged

modules.title: Control output quality and capacity
steps: Run `raven encode` with `--mode zero-width` and `--mode homoglyph` on the same inputs; compare file sizes and note capacity differences
Pass `--stats` on the output to inspect bits-per-character density and Raven's detectability score
Experiment with cover length: try embedding a 500-byte secret in 200 vs 2000 words of cover text and record where Raven warns about low redundancy

modules.title: Decode, verify, and handle failure modes
steps: Send out.txt to yourself by pasting into a plain email body, then run `raven decode --in received.txt --passphrase 'correct horse'`
Test a wrong passphrase and confirm Raven fails cleanly with its HMAC integrity check rather than emitting garbage
Corrupt the carrier deliberately (re-flow line breaks, run through an autocorrecting editor) and identify which edits destroy the payload versus which survive

modules.title: Operational security and anti-detection
steps: Run `raven lint out.txt` to flag residual zero-width characters, trailing whitespace anomalies, and Unicode confusables that scanners catch
Normalize output through `iconv -f UTF-8 -t ASCII//TRANSLIT` and re-run lint to understand why homoglyph mode breaks under normalization
Draft a personal checklist: use long unique passphrases, never reuse the same cover text twice, strip metadata, and match cover register to the channel you post on

prerequisites: Comfortable running CLI tools and piping files
Basic understanding of symmetric encryption and passphrases
Familiarity with UTF-8 text and how editors can alter invisible characters
